newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. fears ethnic persecution in Afghan northwest.
newsitem.headline: U.N. fears ethnic persecution in Afghan northwest.

text.p: The main U.N. refugee agency said on Friday Afghanistan's second major battle in the northwestern province of Badghis seemed to be on ethnic lines and that thousands of people were fleeing from the area.

Refugees continue to flood into the main western city of Herat fleeing from fighting between the mainly Pashtun forces of the radical Islamic Taleban militia and those of Uzbek chief General Abdul Rashid Dostum, a statement by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said.
The battle in Badghis erupted last month after the Taleban captured the capital Kabul on September 27, ousting president Burhanuddin Rabbani's government.

"The fighting and displacement -- which seems to be taking place along ethnic lines -- have been continuing largely unnoticed as a result of the region's remoteness and relative inaccessibility," it said.
The UNHCR said it was not clear if the displacement along ethnic differences was deliberate.

"If deliberate, this would be a very disturbing development indeed. It is a commonly held fear that the conflict in Afghanistan is increasingly leading to the polarisation of the different ethnic groups," the statement said.

"Badghis province was a complex ethnic patchwork, and it seems that ethnic differences have been severely exacerbated by recent military and political developments and that ethnic persecution may have been taking place."

Dostum's jets carried out bombing raids on Friday on the Taleban-held air bases in Herat and Shindand to the south, but there were no reports of any damage, the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press agency said.
The UNHCR said about 800 refugees were arriving daily in Herat, with about 4,000 living in two camps and 2,000 more elsewhere in the city.
Almost all those arriving in Herat are from the Morghab region, 200 km (125 miles) to the north, and virtually all of them are Pashtun, it said.

"As many as 50 percent are nomadic Pashtuns, known as Koochis. Many of them seem to be taking a roundabout route through pistachio forests and across some very rugged terrain... to avoid either the fighting, or forced conscription, or both."

Most of the refugees, including many women and small children, have to travel 100 km (60 miles) or more on foot for five or six days before they reach one of the roads leading to Herat, the UNHCR said.
It quoted those arriving as saying that thousands more were on the move.
It was not clear where the people of non-Pashtun origin had gone, but they could have moved north into Dostum-held Faryab province, the statement said.
"Thousands of Afghan Turkmen have been moving back and forth across the border into Turkmenistan to escape fighting or because they are afraid of persecution."

It said half the population of the Taleban-held Badghis capital of Qala-i-Nau, lying about half-way between Morghab and Herat, had also left. The town had an estimated population of 25,000 before the latest fighting.
